description: We are LOS DEL ESPACIO, building Cocha Digital Twin AI for Cochabamba: reproducible Earth-system evidence from NASA Landsat (LST, NDVI, QA) to detect urban heat and vegetation trends. Skills: software, geospatial data, web/API, analysis. Looking for teammates in Earth science, data viz, ML, and science communication. Join us to turn satellite observations into clear, local insights for the Trend Detective challenge.
summary:
Los del Espacio built a reproducible evidence explorer for one small urban window in Cochabamba, Bolivia. It reads real Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 Collection 2 Level-2 scenes from a public STAC catalog, applies U.S. Geological Survey scale factors and a shared quality mask, and calculates land-surface temperature in degrees Celsius and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index. The pilot keeps one July scene from each of 2022, 2023, and 2024. A local API and web app map those observations in 2D and 3D, compare the three dates, and export CSV and JSON with the source, scene identifier, method, valid coverage, and empty cells.

This answers Be An Earth System Trend Detective by showing change in place and time without calling three clear-sky dates a climate trend. The app does not report a slope, a confidence interval, or a significance test. Land-surface temperature is labeled as surface temperature. Missing pixels stay missing.

Cochabamba needs that discipline before any district score or forecast. The result is an evidence path with its limits on screen. It is a pilot, not a validated digital twin or a prediction model.
details:
What it does

LOS DEL ESPACIO is a local evidence pipeline for Cochabamba. It turns real satellite scenes into a map, a date comparison, and a downloadable record. The study area is one small rectangle inside the city. It is not the municipal boundary and it is not an official district.

How it works

The pipeline queries the public Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 STAC catalog and reads five bands for one low-cloud July scene in 2022, 2023, and 2024. It applies the U.S. Geological Survey scale and offset, masks clouds and saturated pixels, and calculates land-surface temperature in degrees Celsius and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index on the same valid pixels. Map cells are averages of about 360 meters. A validated snapshot is served by a local API. The web explorer shows the cells in 2D and 3D, compares the three dates, and exports CSV and JSON with scene identifiers, method, valid coverage, and empty values where pixels fail quality control.

Benefits and intended impact

A resident or a municipal analyst can see where the surface was warmer or greener on those three dates, and can trace every number to a scene and a method. Empty cells stay empty. The same limits are written in the interface: three clear-sky dates are a description, not a climate trend, and land-surface temperature is not air temperature. That standard is the useful result. Later district scores or forecasts can be added only when official boundaries and a longer comparable series exist.

Tools

Python, a typed scientific ingest script, FastAPI, Pydantic, Alembic, and PostGIS store and serve the evidence. Next.js, React, and TypeScript provide the explorer. Docker Compose runs the local stack. Tests use pytest and Playwright. Landsat windows are read as cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs. The basemap is OpenStreetMap.

Creativity and design choices

The team treated a missing answer as a valid result. The product shows provenance, quality masks, and sample size instead of a single score. Synthetic rectangles used in development are labeled as demos and are not offered as the 15 official districts. A municipal PM10 import path is in the repository; those records are not presented as validated observations and are not used to calibrate land-surface temperature, because station coordinates, time zone, and license are still incomplete. No live language-model call runs inside the explorer.

Super Intelligence disclosure

Team members used Cursor and OpenAI Codex, which are large language models, to draft, review, and revise code, tests, and documentation. People checked the scientific limits against the Landsat method. No image, video, or audio file in the project was generated by an SI tool. This submission text was drafted with an SI assistant for the team to review before sending.
